title: The Expedition of Muʿtah (Jumādā al-Ūlā 8 AH)
owner_gate: compiled 2026-10-27 for the Muʿtah model; ledger remains awaiting owner review
app_target: 3D Seerah learning app for ages 12-25 (interactive 3D scenes; battle timeline; verse overlays)

spine_source.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Saifur Rahman al-Mubarakpuri, trans. Issam Diab (Dar-us-Salam)
spine_source.file: Muʿtah chapter read this session through the publisher-authorized online copy at rasoulallah.net (article 1888); the local PDF was not re-read
spine_source.mutah_chapter_pages: not page-verified this session — the online copy carries the same chapter text and its own footnotes (Za'd al-Ma'ad 2/155-156; Fath al-Bari 7/511-514)
spine_source.citation_format: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)

grading_note: Graded 2026-10-27 against live hadith pages (Sahih al-Bukhari 4261-4266; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3763), api.alquran.cloud (3:169; 19:71), and two independent sirah retellings. The canonical hadith carry the command succession, the three deaths, the Prophet's announcement and tears, Khalid's nine swords and Ja'far's two-winged title. The casus belli, the 3,000, the enemy numbers, the night ruse and the twelve martyrs are sirah-only and are graded REPORTED. The outcome framing is DISPUTED and must never be harmonised: Bukhari says Allah made them victorious; the sirah says the army withdrew without avenging the envoy.

conventions.block_tagging: Same as badr.json: all entries HISTORY; no reflections in this phase.
conventions.honorifics: The Prophet is referenced as 'the Prophet (PBUH)' in rendered text; Companions carry honorifics at first mention per block. No figural depiction of the Prophet (PBUH) or any face.
conventions.quote_cap: Direct on-screen quotes <= 15 words; Quran fetched live from api.alquran.cloud.
conventions.no_harmonization: DISPUTED entries display ranges/both versions, never merged. UNKNOWN = not yet verifiable this session; hidden by default.
conventions.secondary_sirah: Ibn Hisham/Ibn Ishaq- and al-Waqidi-derived claims are cited via the Raheeq chapter or the logged retellings; no full Guillaume or al-Waqidi translation is owned locally.

grading_policy.CERTAIN: >= 2 independent sources, at least one canonical (Quran > Sahih Bukhari/Muslim > other canonical collections > sirah Ibn Hisham/Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabari > modern critical works). Raheeq al-Makhtum alone never certifies.
grading_policy.REPORTED: Solid single-chain sirah/hadith detail; accurate to attribute but from one lineage or modern retelling only; rendered with no certainty implied.
grading_policy.DISPUTED: Transmitted variants conflict; app must show ranges/both versions, never harmonized.
grading_policy.UNKNOWN: Cannot be verified from owned + live sources; never rendered without user approval.

render_as_policy.solid: Canonical or >=2 independent sources; safe as primary on-screen facts, may carry direct quotes.
render_as_policy.approx: Reported or contested detail; render visually/ambiguously, quotes flagged, no claim of certainty.
render_as_policy.hidden: Do not render in current phase; visible only in an app 'scholar's mode' if the user approves.

verse_anchors.text_en_sahih: And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision,
verse_anchors.note: The general verse of the martyrs. It is conventionally recited for Muʿtah and for all the fallen; the sources do not make it Muʿtah-specific, so the model renders it as a bridge at the memorial, not as an occasion-of-revelation claim.

verse_anchors.text_en_sahih: And there is none of you except he will come to it. This is upon your Lord an inevitability decreed.
verse_anchors.note: The verse ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah is reported to have quoted when he wept at the farewell (MUT-005). The verse is verified; the attribution to that moment is sirah-only.

entries.claim: The expedition took place in Jumādā al-Ūlā 8 AH (September 629) at Muʿtah, a village in al-Balqāʾ on the edge of geographical Syria, in what is now Jordan near al-Karak.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: Jumada al-ula 8 A.H. / september 629 A.D. ... Mu'tah is a village that lies on the borders of geographical Syria
near the village of Mutah (currently located near the city of Karak in Jordan)

variants.note: The month is given consistently as Jumādā al-Ūlā in the live retellings; the Gregorian conversion (September 629) is conventional. No canonical hadith fixes the date.

entries.notes: Phase divider: 'Jumādā al-Ūlā, 8 AH · Muʿtah, al-Balqāʾ'. No day-number asserted.

entries.claim: The Prophet (PBUH) had sent al-Ḥārith ibn ʿUmayr al-Azdī with a letter to the ruler of Buṣrā. On the road, Shuraḥbīl ibn ʿAmr al-Ghassānī, the governor of al-Balqāʾ and a Byzantine ally, intercepted and killed him.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: intercepted by sharhabeel bin 'amr al-ghassani, the governor of al-balqa'
intercepted and killed by Shurahbil bin 'Amr Al-Ghassani
Al-Harith (R.A.) was intercepted by Shurahbil bin Amrul-Ghassani

variants.note: The envoy's murder is the reported casus belli; it rests on the sirah (al-Waqidi is the earliest detailed source) and has no canonical hadith chain. The spelling Shuraḥbīl / Shurahbil / Sharhabeel varies; the glossary fixes Shuraḥbīl ibn ʿAmr al-Ghassānī.

entries.notes: On the road-north label only. No depiction of the killing; a cairn and a text label carry it.

entries.claim: Grieved by the envoy's death, the Prophet (PBUH) mobilised 3,000 men for the north and gave the white banner to Zayd ibn Ḥārithah.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: a large army of 3000 men be mobilized
an army ... consisted of 3,000 Muslims

variants.note: The 3,000 is sirah-only; the appointment and succession are canonical (MUT-004), but the canonical text does not give the army's size. Do not print 'largest army' as a graded claim.

entries.notes: Crowd staging: 3,000 instanced men, labelled 'about 3,000 · reported'.

entries.claim: The Prophet (PBUH) appointed Zayd ibn Ḥārithah as commander and said that if Zayd were killed, Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib should take over, and if Jaʿfar were killed, ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah.

sources.quote: If Zaid is martyred, Ja'far should take over his position
Zaid took the flag ... then Ja'far took it ... then Ibn Rawaha took it

entries.notes: The command-succession backbone. Three named standards, no named figures.

entries.claim: The army bade farewell at Madinah. ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah wept and said it was not love of the world but the verse 'there is none of you except he will come to it' (19:71); he said the party had come out seeking martyrdom.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: nor under a motive of infatuation with the glamour of life
And there is none of you except he will come to it
Abdullah bin Rawaha began to weep at that moment

variants.note: The verse is canonical; the weeping scene and its explanation are sirah (Ibn Hishām/al-Wāqidī lineage). Render the verse as a verified anchor and the scene as reported.

entries.notes: A label at the south road in the march phase; no figure.

entries.claim: The Prophet (PBUH) instructed the army to fight in Allah's name without treachery or breach of covenant, not to kill a newborn, a woman, an aged man or a hermit, and not to cut trees or demolish homes.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: neither breach a covenant nor entertain treachery
under no circumstances a new-born, woman, an ageing man or a hermit should be killed

variants.note: This dispatch wording is sirah. Its substance (the protected non-combatants) is echoed in canonical war ethics, but no canonical chain carries this exact Muʿtah instruction; keep it REPORTED and quote within the cap.

entries.notes: Ethics beat for the march: 'no treachery · no women, children or aged'.

entries.claim: At Maʿān, on the Syrian border, news came that Heraclius had gathered 100,000 Byzantine troops and 100,000 men of Lakhm, Judhām, al-Qayn, Bahra and Balī. The Muslims had not expected a host of that size.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: a hundred thousand troops together with another hundred thousand men
100,000 Greeks joined by 100,000 men from Lakhm, Judham, Al-Qayn, Bahra and Bali

variants.note: The reports give 200,000 (100,000 Byzantine + 100,000 allied) as the common figure; some retellings speak of 100,000 in total. No canonical hadith gives a count. The model renders 'reports say 100,000–200,000' and stages a maquette host, never a literal 200,000.
The staging of a 6,000-man instanced mass is a design compression, not a historical count.

entries.notes: Enemy unit label: 'the enemy host · reports say 100,000–200,000'.

entries.claim: The Muslims spent two nights debating whether to write to Madinah for orders. ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah urged them on: what they disliked was the very thing they had come seeking — martyrdom; they fought with the religion Allah had honoured them with, and either victory or martyrdom was good.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: dart to win either of the two, victory or martyrdom
Both prospects are fine: Victory or martyrdom

entries.notes: Label beat only; quote within 15 words: 'Victory or martyrdom' (3 words) may render with attribution.

entries.claim: The army moved to Mashārif in al-Balqāʾ, then withdrew to Muʿtah and encamped. Qutbah ibn Qatādah al-ʿUdhrī led the right wing and ʿUbādah (or Ubayyah) ibn Mālik al-Anṣārī the left.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: changed direction towards Mu'tah where they encamped
the right wing led by Qutbah Ibn Qatadah

variants.note: The wing commanders' names rest on the sirah alone and the left commander's name varies (ʿUbādah / Ubayyah / ʿUbaydah). Keep them off the model's labels unless the owner approves; the wing positions are staged without names.

entries.notes: Hidden: no on-screen names for the wings; the formations carry the shape.

entries.claim: The field is a stony upland plain in al-Balqāʾ: the village of Muʿtah on a low rise, a shallow wādī between the two hosts, olive country and dry wheat stubble, with the highlands of geographical Syria beyond.

sources.quote: near the village of Mutah (currently located near the city of Karak in Jordan)

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: Mu'tah is a village that lies on the borders of geographical Syria

variants.note: The wādī, the olive groves and the stubble are a terrain stylisation keyed to the Balqāʾ highlands, not a survey. No source describes the battle-day ground in detail; no on-screen claim of a surveyed site.

entries.notes: Terrain brief for the heightfield: pale limestone, dry wādī, olive groves, village tell, distant ridges.

entries.claim: Zayd ibn Ḥārithah carried the standard and was killed. The sirah says he fell among the spears, bleeding, still advancing.

sources.quote: Zaid took the flag ... and was martyred

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: until he fell, fatally stabbed
died from loss of blood among the spears of the enemy

variants.note: The death is canonical; the manner (spears, blood loss) is sirah detail and is rendered as a fallen standard, not a wound effect.

entries.notes: First standard falls. No figure; no blood.

entries.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib took the standard after Zayd and was killed. He was found among the fallen with many wounds, none of them in his back.

sources.quote: then Ja'far took it and was martyred
he counted fifty wounds in his body ... none of those wounds was in his back

variants.note: The same hadith reports 'over ninety wounds' in the second half of Ibn ʿUmar's account; the two counts sit side by side in the transmitted text. The model says 'fifty wounds counted' and flags the other count in the ledger, not on screen.

entries.notes: Second standard falls. The 'none in his back' line is the moral centre: he did not turn.

entries.claim: In the sirah's account, Jaʿfar's right hand was cut off, then his left; he clasped the standard with his arms until he was killed. He is reported to have refused water while fasting.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: until his right hand was cut off ... he clasped the banner with both arms
until it was cut off. He seized the standard with his left hand until that too was cut off

variants.note: The arm sequence is sirah, not in the canonical hadith. Do not stage a graphic amputation; the falling standard carries the beat. The refused-water detail is single-retelling and stays off screen.

entries.notes: Label: 'the standard is cut from his hands · reported'.

entries.claim: ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah took the standard after Jaʿfar and was killed, fighting on horseback and reciting verses.

sources.quote: then Ibn Rawaha took it and was martyred

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: fight bravely on his horseback while reciting enthusiastic verses

variants.note: The death is canonical; the horse and the verses are sirah. No verse text is rendered.

entries.notes: Third standard falls.

entries.claim: The Prophet (PBUH) told the people in Madinah of the three deaths before the news arrived, and his eyes shed tears. He said the flag was then taken by 'a sword among the swords of Allah' — Khalid — and that Allah made them victorious.

sources.quote: At that time the Prophet's eyes were shedding tears
a Sword amongst the Swords of Allah (i.e. Khalid) and Allah made them victorious

variants.note: 'Allah made them victorious' sits in the same canonical report as the withdrawal narrative of MUT-017; the model shows both and does not resolve them (MUT-018).

entries.notes: The home-front announcement and the Sword of Allah title. No depiction; labels only.

entries.claim: Khalid ibn al-Walīd took the banner after the three commanders fell. He reported that nine swords broke in his hand that day and only a Yemeni sword remained.

sources.quote: nine swords were broken in my hand, and nothing was left ... except a Yemenite sword
Then the flag was taken by a Sword amongst the Swords of Allah

entries.notes: Signature beat: nine broken swords on the ground around the rising standard. Weapon-masses only.

entries.claim: At night Khalid shifted the flanks and brought up the rear so that at dawn the enemy saw what looked like fresh reinforcements. The Byzantines hesitated, and the Muslims withdrew in order toward Madinah rather than press the field.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: reshuffled the right and left flanks ... a fully organized and well-planned withdrawal
Khalid positioned his men in such a way that they appeared to look greater in number

variants.note: The ruse is sirah (Ibn Isḥāq/al-Wāqidī); no canonical hadith describes it. The hadith's 'Allah made them victorious' (MUT-015) is not a description of a battlefield rout; the model stages the ordered withdrawal and labels both reports (MUT-018).

entries.notes: Night-to-dawn beat; the army pulls back, the enemy holds. No rout.

entries.claim: The outcome is framed two ways in the transmitted material. The canonical report says Allah made the Muslims victorious. The sirah says the army withdrew to Madinah and did not avenge the envoy, and presents the expedition as a strategic success in reputation rather than a conquest.

sources.quote: Allah made them (i.e. the Muslims) victorious

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: the battle did not satisfy the muslims' objective, namely avenging al-harith's murder

variants.note: Victory-side: Bukhari 4262. Withdrawal-side: the sirah's ordered retreat and unmet objective (Raheeq; IslamicFinder). The model must show both, never merge them into 'a victory' or 'a defeat'.

entries.notes: Labels: 'the report calls it a victory' and 'the army withdraws in order' — both visible in the withdrawal phase.

entries.claim: The Muslims lost twelve men, according to the sirah; some retellings say fifteen. Byzantine losses are not given, though the reports describe them as heavy.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: the muslims sustained twelve martyrs
The Muslims sustained twelve martyrs (some sources say 15)

variants.note: Twelve is the common figure; fifteen appears in some retellings. Byzantine casualties are unknown. The memorial shows twelve stones and the label 'twelve by the reports'.

entries.notes: Memorial stones at the field; no body count claim for the enemy.

entries.claim: Jaʿfar (RA) became known as 'the two-winged one': Ibn ʿUmar used to greet Jaʿfar's son with 'Peace be upon you, O son of the two-winged person.'

sources.quote: O the son of two-winged person
I saw Ja'far flying in Paradise with the angels

entries.notes: The title is canonical in two collections. Render the title at the memorial, never as depicted wings.

entries.claim: The Prophet (PBUH) reported seeing Jaʿfar flying in Paradise with the angels; other reports say his two wings were dyed with blood.

sources.quote: I saw Ja'far flying in Paradise with the angels
Your father is flying with the Angels in the sky

variants.note: The flying vision is a single canonical chain (Tirmidhi 3763); the blood-dyed wings detail is in al-Ḥākim and al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr, graded ḥasan by Ibn Ḥajar and al-Haythamī. Keep REPORTED; no visual wings.

entries.notes: Label only: 'Jaʿfar (RA) · the two wings'.

entries.claim: When the news reached Madinah, the Prophet (PBUH) sat with sorrow plain on his face; ʿĀ'ishah described it, and the women of Jaʿfar were weeping.

sources.quote: Allah's Apostle sat with sorrow explicit on his face

entries.notes: Sober home-front beat; no depiction, no re-enactment of the weeping.

entries.claim: The Prophet (PBUH) went to Jaʿfar's house, comforted his wife Asmā' bint ʿUmays, cared for Jaʿfar's sons for three days, and went out to meet the returning army with ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaʿfar riding with him at Juruf outside Madinah.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: he went out to meet it with 'Abdullah riding with him
He kept them with him for three days
gathered at a place called Juruf, outside Madinah

variants.note: The household and Juruf details are sirah (Ibn Sa'd/Ibn Hishām lineage); Bukhari 4263 independently attests the Prophet's sorrow and the weeping household, not the three days or the meeting. No depiction of the Prophet (PBUH).

entries.notes: Labels on the south road only: 'the army returns' and 'the Prophet (PBUH) meets them · reported'.

entries.claim: The expedition did not take a city or avenge the envoy, but it checked the northern tribes, raised the Muslims' reputation on the Byzantine frontier, and preceded the later northern campaigns.

sources.work: Raheeq al-Makhtum (MSA NIU English ed.), Muʿtah chapter (online copy)
sources.quote: it resulted in a far-ranging impact
it resulted in a far-ranging impact and attached to the Muslims a great reputation

variants.note: This is the sirah's retrospective assessment, not a canonical claim; keep it as a closing note, not as a scoreline.

entries.notes: Closing label: 'the northern road stays open · reported'.
